PUBLIC RESPONSE: Agency Law (first explicit statutory reference appears in its s. 1, predating the later codification of good faith in the 1973 Contracts Law)

The modern Israeli civil-law codification programme began in the mid-1960s. The earliest statute enacted within that programme that expressly imported the continental-style “good faith” (tom lev / bona fides) standard is the Agency Law, 1965. Its opening section states that agency relations are governed, inter alia, “by the rules of good faith and diligence,” thereby introducing the concept into positive Israeli legislation for the first time. Subsequent enactments (Sales Law 1968, Contracts (General Part) Law 1973, etc.) built upon this precedent, but none predates 1965.

The modern Israeli legal system began developing original statutes in the mid-1960s as part of a systematic civil-code project. Among the early enactments (Succession Law 1965, Agency Law 1965, Bailees Law 1967), none contained the phrase “good faith.” The Sale Law 1968 was the first to do so, stating in §6 that a contract of sale must be performed “in good faith and in the customary manner.” Subsequent statutes (Contracts (Remedies) Law 1970, Contracts (General Part) Law 1973, etc.) reused and expanded the term, confirming that the 1968 Sale Law introduced it.
